desc:
Two subtrees (a node together with all its descendants) are the same if they are identical in shape and in every node value. Count how many distinct subtrees occur at two or more different nodes of the given tree. Each distinct repeated subtree is counted once, however many copies exist. Leaves are subtrees too.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 2, 3, -1, 3] the answer is 2: the subtree 'a lone 3' appears twice, and the subtree 'a 2 with a single left child 3' appears twice. The root is unique.
constraints: Every tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Comparing every pair of subtrees node by node is far too slow. Can a subtree be described by something short that is equal for equal subtrees?
Describe a subtree by its root value together with descriptions of its left and right subtrees (and mark missing children). Two subtrees are equal exactly when their descriptions are equal.

Replace the long text description by a small integer id: look up the triple (value, left id, right id) in a dictionary shared by all nodes, creating a new id when it is new. Count how many nodes get each id and count the ids that occur at least twice.
editorial: Serialising every subtree as a string works but may cost O(n2) characters on chain-shaped trees. The fix is to avoid repeating the work for the children: if each child subtree already has a small integer id, the identity of a node is just the triple (value, leftId, rightId) with id 0 for a missing child.

Process the nodes bottom-up and keep a dictionary from triples to ids. Two subtrees get the same id exactly when they are identical, by induction on the height. Count the occurrences of every id (a Counter) and return the number of ids occurring at least twice. Counting ids instead of nodes is what makes each repeated shape count once.
Every node does one dictionary lookup, so the time is O(n) expected, and the dictionary holds at most n entries.
